# What "learning" means {#sec-ch01}

::: {.epigraph by="Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1984"}
The question of whether a computer can think is no more interesting than the question of whether a submarine can swim.
:::

AI. Machine learning. Deep learning. LLMs. RAG. Agents. If you're getting into AI, these words are everywhere, and it can feel like seven separate subjects to learn.

They're not. They're chapters of one story, and each exists because the one before it hit a problem it couldn't solve. This chapter tells that story from the start, and ends with where this book fits in it.

::: {.goals}
- Tell the difference between a computer following rules and a computer learning.
- Say what a *model* is, in one plain sentence.
- See why a machine can learn exactly what you asked and still be useless.
- Place AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs, RAG, agents and Jev on one map.
:::

## Start with a rule

Inside a thermostat is a line that says, more or less: *if the temperature is above 30°C, turn on the fan.*

That's a computer following a rule. Someone told it exactly what to do. It works nothing out.

A lot of software called "AI" is no more than this. A bank blocks payments over a limit. A spam filter deletes any email containing "lottery". And rules are *good*: fast, cheap, and when one goes wrong you can read why. When a rule does the job, use it. In Chapter 13, plain rules beat far more complex models in more than one round.

The trouble starts when the world changes faster than you can write rules.

## When rules run out

A company's security team wants to catch *phishing*: emails that trick staff into typing their password into a fake page. Someone writes the obvious rule: *if an email mentions "password", flag it.*

On Monday it flags the IT team's own password-reset emails, so they add an exception. On Wednesday an attacker writes "passw0rd" with a zero. Another rule. On Friday the attacker drops the word completely and sends a link to a fake shared document.

![Two ways to catch phishing. On the left, every new trick forces a new exception, and the list never catches up. On the right, we stop writing rules and show the computer labelled examples instead.](/figures/ch01/rules-vs-examples.pdf){#fig-rules-vs-examples}

The list of rules grows, and it's always one trick behind (@fig-rules-vs-examples). The attacker can learn your rules by testing them. You can't read theirs.

## Let the examples write the rules

So turn the job around. Give the computer thousands of emails where the answer is already known, *this one was phishing, this one was fine*, and let it find the pattern that separates them.

::: {.keyidea}
**Machine learning** is getting a computer to work out the rules itself, from examples where the answer is already known.
:::

It has been deciding things about you for years. When your bank texts *"Did you just spend ₹40,000 at an electronics shop in another city?"*, nobody wrote a rule about you. A system learned what your normal spending looks like, and this payment didn't fit.

## So what's a "model"?

When the learning is done, it leaves something behind: a thing that takes an input and gives an answer. Give it an email, it says "phishing" or "fine". That thing is the model.

Picture a machine with many knobs. Learning means turning the knobs until the machine gets the examples right as often as possible. Then you stop turning and use it on new cases, where nobody knows the answer yet.

::: {.keyidea}
A **model** is a function whose settings came from examples rather than from a programmer.
:::

## A machine learns, and learns the wrong thing

Now a real example. Our security team belongs to a made-up shipping company, Kestrel Logistics. In four weeks it receives {{< num ch01 n_alerts int >}} alerts, about {{< num ch01 per_day int >}} a day. Only {{< num ch01 base_rate pct1 >}} are real attacks; the rest are false alarms. (The company and its alerts are invented by a program, so we know the true answer for every one. That lets us check every model's work exactly.)

Each alert comes with a *threat score* between 0 and 1: how dangerous outside security sources think the sender or website is. An obvious rule: *flag the alert if its score is at least some number t.* A number like that, which splits cases into two groups, is a **threshold**.

Which *t*? We don't guess. We let the machine try every value from 0 to 1, count the mistakes each one makes, and keep the one with the fewest. That's learning in its smallest form: *try settings, count mistakes, keep the best.*

![Every possible threshold and the mistakes it makes. Low thresholds bury the team in false alarms; high ones miss attacks. The total is lowest at the far right, just below the dotted line for "flag nothing at all".](/figures/ch01/threshold-search.pdf){#fig-threshold-search}

The machine picks {{< num ch01 best_t f2 >}}: it flags only the very worst scores. It makes {{< num ch01 best_mistakes int >}} mistakes. A "rule" that never flags anything makes {{< num ch01 never_flag_mistakes int >}}, barely more. Of {{< num ch01 attacks int >}} real attacks, the winning rule catches {{< num ch01 best_caught int >}}.

Why? Harmless alerts outnumber attacks about twelve to one. So every false alarm hurts the mistake count more than catching an attack helps it, and the search pushes the threshold up until the rule almost stops raising alarms (@fig-threshold-search).

The machine did exactly what we asked. We asked the wrong question.

::: {.keyidea}
A model learns exactly what you ask for: ask the wrong question, and it learns the wrong thing.
:::

Two things went wrong. First, we counted every mistake as equal, but missing a real attack and wasting five minutes of someone's time are not equal. Chapter 4 fixes that. Second, and this is what the book is really about, we forced the answer to be *yes* or *no*.

::: {.breaks}
A model only knows the world its examples came from. If attackers invent a new trick, the model has never seen it, and its answer will look just as confident as always. Labels can be wrong too: some attacks are never found, so they sit in the data marked "fine", and the model learns that mistake as if it were true.
:::

## The answer isn't yes or no

Ask a better question: *among alerts with a given score, how many turned out to be attacks?*

![Group the alerts by threat score and count how many were real attacks. The share climbs steadily from 2% to 62%. Even at the top, plenty are harmless; even at the bottom, a few are attacks.](/figures/ch01/not-yes-no.pdf){#fig-not-yes-no}

There's no point where alerts switch from harmless to dangerous (@fig-not-yes-no). Among the lowest scores, about {{< num ch01 bottom_bin_rate pct >}} were attacks. That sounds tiny, but it's {{< num ch01 bottom_bin_n int >}} alerts, so over a hundred attacks hide among the most harmless-looking ones. Among the highest scores, {{< num ch01 top_bin_rate pct >}} were attacks, so more than a third of the scariest-looking alerts were nothing.

So what do we know about an alert scoring 0.55? Not "attack". Not "fine". We know *about one in five alerts like this is an attack.*

That number tells the team how worried to be. It lets them check the likeliest attacks first. And once they know what each mistake costs, it tells them where to draw the line.

::: {.keyidea}
A good model doesn't just answer: it says how sure it is, and it's right about how sure it is.
:::

Being *right about how sure it is* has a name: **calibration**. It's a different goal from "make the fewest mistakes", and Chapter 3 is all about it.

::: {.threshold}
Missing a real attack costs the company about ten times what a false alarm costs. Should the threshold go *up* from {{< num ch01 best_t f2 >}} or *down*?

(Down, a lot. When a miss hurts more, you accept more false alarms to avoid one. Chapter 4 turns this into a formula.)
:::

## The rest of the story

A threat score is one handy number. But a photo is millions of pixels and an email is a string of words; nobody can hand-write the clues for "this sounds like a scam". So the next step was models that learn their own clues, in many stacked layers: **deep learning** (Chapter 5).

Train a huge deep-learning model on a huge amount of text, with one task, *guess the next word*, and it picks up grammar, facts and some reasoning along the way. That's a **large language model**, or LLM (Chapter 6).

An LLM knows a lot about the world and nothing about *your* world, so we let it look things up before it answers: **retrieval-augmented generation**, or RAG. And once a model can read, we want it to *act*: check a log, block an account, choose the next step. A model working in that loop is an **agent** (Chapter 7).

## Where this book fits

Watch an agent work and you notice something. Most of its steps aren't writing. They're small decisions with a few possible answers. *Is this alert real? Which team gets this ticket? Is this action safe?*

Today, each of those usually goes to an LLM, which writes a paragraph, and then more code digs the answer out of the paragraph. It works. It's also like hiring a novelist to tick a checkbox.

![The same question, two ways. An LLM writes its answer piece by piece, and your code has to read the sentence. A decision model returns the answer as data, with a probability for every option, in one pass.](/figures/ch01/generate-vs-decide.pdf){#fig-generate-vs-decide}

In September 2026 a start-up, TypeSafe AI, released **Jev**, a model built only for those checkbox moments. It never writes text. You give it a situation and a typed question, "pick one of these labels" or "yes or no?", and it returns the answer as data, with a probability for every option (@fig-generate-vs-decide). TypeSafe calls it a *System One* model, after the psychologist Daniel Kahneman's name for fast, intuitive thinking [@kahneman2011].

One honest note. I had no access to Jev's API while writing, so every Jev answer in this book comes from a stand-in I built that copies Jev's public interface. Those numbers are marked *synthetic*. Asked about one alert, an overnight flood of sign-in requests, the stand-in says {{< num ch01 mock_p_99 f2 >}}: probably an attack. It wasn't. That isn't a failure. A 0.68 is a claim that *about two in three alerts like this* are attacks; this one was in the other third. Whether a model's 0.68 really means two in three is something we can test, and Chapters 3 and 11 do.

![The story so far. Each step exists because the one before it hit a problem it couldn't solve. System One models like Jev grow out of deep learning and fit into the "decide" step of an agent.](/figures/ch01/ai-story-map.pdf){#fig-ai-story-map}

That's the whole map (@fig-ai-story-map). Rules weren't enough, so machines learned from examples. Models grew, learned language, then learned to look things up and to act. And inside those loops, most of the work turned out to be *deciding*: quickly, cheaply, with probabilities that honestly say how sure they are.

The next three chapters stay at the bottom of that map on purpose, because everything above it rests on one idea: an answer should be a probability, and the probability should mean what it says.

::: {.exercises}
1. Name one system you use every week that follows rules, and one that learned from examples. What gave each away?
2. Our best rule made {{< num ch01 best_mistakes int >}} mistakes and caught almost nothing. Write one sentence for the question you *wish* we had asked the machine instead.
:::

::: {.nexthook}
Next: "how likely" sounds like a small change. It's the most important idea in the book, and it hides a trap that fools doctors, judges and security teams.
:::
